Pernicious
pẽr-nĭsh´ŭs
adj. (destructive; having the quality of killing or ruining, often slowly and without alarm)
Latin perniciosus, from per-, thoroughly, and nex, death. The AV uses it once, of the ways false teachers make popular (2Pe 2:2).

Definition · Scriptures · Corruption · Roots · Usage · Related

Biblical Definition

Pernicious means quietly destructive. Peter's use is of doctrine that spreads: false teachers “shall bring in damnable heresies, even denying the Lord that bought them… and many shall follow their pernicious ways; by reason of whom the way of truth shall be evil spoken of” (2Pe 2:1–2). Paul warns the Ephesian elders that “grievous wolves” shall enter in, not sparing the flock, and that some shall arise from among their own selves (Act 20:29–30). The Lord notes the disguise: false prophets come “in sheep's clothing, but inwardly they are ravening wolves” (Mat 7:15). And the spread is like disease: “their word will eat as doth a canker” (2Ti 2:17).

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster (1828) defines pernicious as destructive; having the quality of killing, destroying or injuring; very injurious or mischievous.

expand to see more

PERNICIOUS, a. Destructive; having the quality of killing, destroying or injuring; very injurious or mischievous.

Sin is pernicious to the soul, as well as to the body.

2. Quick. [Not in use.]

PERNICIOUSLY, adv. Destructively; with ruinous tendency.

Key Scripture

2Pe 2:1 — "But there were false prophets also among the people, even as there shall be false teachers among you, who privily shall bring in damnable heresies, even denying the Lord that bought them, and bring upon themselves swift destruction."

2Pe 2:2 — "And many shall follow their pernicious ways; by reason of whom the way of truth shall be evil spoken of."

Act 20:29 — "For I know this, that after my departing shall grievous wolves enter in among you, not sparing the flock."

Mat 7:15 — "Beware of false prophets, which come to you in sheep's clothing, but inwardly they are ravening wolves."

2Ti 2:17 — "And their word will eat as doth a canker: of whom is Hymenaeus and Philetus;"

Modern Corruption

Error is expected to arrive looking dangerous, and the pernicious kind arrives looking attractive and popular.

expand to see more

Second Peter 2:2 contains a detail that ought to be read aloud in every discussion of doctrinal drift: many shall follow their pernicious ways. Not a fringe, not a handful — many. Ruinous teaching does not survive by being obviously ruinous; it survives by being appealing, and the size of the following is no evidence at all about its soundness. A church that measures a ministry by its growth has adopted the one metric this verse explicitly refuses.

Acts 20:30 supplies the harder half of the warning. Paul tells the Ephesian elders that grievous wolves will come in from outside, and then says also of your own selves shall men arise, speaking perverse things, to draw away disciples after them. The danger is not only external. It comes from the eldership, from men the congregation trusts, and the motive named is the drawing away of disciples after them — a following of one's own. That is why the discipline of watching doctrine cannot be delegated entirely to the men being watched.

Second Timothy 2:17 gives the pathology in one image: their word will eat as doth a canker — a gangrene, spreading through living tissue, painless at the edge. That is the difference between a heresy and a pernicious teaching. A frontal denial of the resurrection provokes resistance; a slow reweighting of emphases, a doctrine quietly dropped from the preaching, a category of sin no longer named, meets none. The remedy Paul prescribes in the same chapter is unspectacular: a workman rightly dividing the word of truth, and a man who departs from iniquity.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Greek apoleia (G684), destruction, perdition; hairesis (G139), heresy, a chosen party; lukos barus (G3074), grievous wolf; gaggraina (G1044), a canker, gangrene.

expand to see more

Greek apoleia (G684) — destruction; 2 Peter 2:1–3, Philippians 3:19, Matthew 7:13 — rendered both damnable and pernicious in 2 Peter 2.

Greek hairesis (G139) — heresy; 2 Peter 2:1, Galatians 5:20, Titus 3:10.

Greek gaggraina (G1044) — gangrene, canker; 2 Timothy 2:17 only.

Usage

"“Many shall follow their pernicious ways” — many, and that is the point."

"“Of your own selves shall men arise” — said to an eldership."

"“Their word will eat as doth a canker” — painless at the edge."
